CausalChain: HBV/HCV infection or other inflammatory stimuli -> increased IL-6 secretion in liver microenvironment -> IL-6 binds to IL-6R/gp130 -> Activation of JAK leading to STAT3 phosphorylation -> STAT3 dimerizes and translocates to the nucleus -> Upregulation of oncogenic targets including AFP and cancer stem cell markers -> AFP further contributes to suppression of p53 and possibly reinforces IL-6/STAT3 signaling via autocrine/paracrine feedback -> Enhanced tumor cell proliferation, survival, drug resistance, and metastasis.
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that disrupting the feed‐forward loop between AFP expression and the IL-6/STAT3 signaling axis will restore p53 tumor suppressor activity and diminish the stemness and chemoresistance of HCC cells, providing a promising new target for therapeutic intervention.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) development is characterized by complex interactions between inflammatory signals and oncogenic pathways, with the IL‐6/STAT3 signaling axis playing a central role. In the chronically inflamed liver, virus‐induced elevation of IL‐6 activates STAT3 through canonical receptor-mediated cascades, leading to upregulation of genes involved in proliferation, anti‐apoptosis, angiogenesis, and cancer stem cell maintenance. Notably, STAT3 activation also promotes alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) expression, which has been implicated in HCC progression and drug resistance, in part by dampening p53 tumor suppressor activity and fostering a feed-forward loop that enhances malignant phenotypes. Here, we propose that disruption of the AFP-mediated reinforcement of the IL-6/STAT3 pathway may serve as a novel therapeutic target, potentially restoring p53 function and reducing the stem-like, chemoresistant properties of HCC cells. Targeted inhibition of this feedback loop might therefore counteract tumor progression and improve response to conventional therapies.
